A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same responsiveness-metric research. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original analyses of image-safety ratings and toxicity comments, plus scoring-pattern simulations, in Section 5 and Appendices C and H.

after.justification: v5 reports original analyses of both retained datasets, revised crowd-reference comparisons and scoring-pattern simulations in Section 5 and Appendix D.

M1.justification: v5 Section 4.2 adds a zero floor for negative MPA values, changing the stated boundary-case calculation. The underlying MPA, WRA and harmonic-mean construction remains stable. However, the supplied code still lacks this floor, so a corresponding implementation change is not established.

E1.justification: Both versions use the image-safety dataset, the 107,620-comment toxicity dataset, the same demographic axes and the same three simulated scoring patterns. The toxicity study moves from v2 Appendix H into v5 Section 5; it is not new coverage.

E2.justification: v5 adds IRT Graded Response Model discrimination to the toxicity comparison, alongside the retained Kendall's tau and AUROC comparators (v2 Figure 12; v5 Figure 3). IRT and Mokken already participated in the image crowd-reference comparison.

E3.justification: The image crowd-reference experiment changes from micro- to macro-averaging across thresholds. Toxicity replaces a leave-group-out median thresholded at 2 with individual reference ratings binarized at boundaries 1–4 and macro-averaged. The simulation description also replaces additive item-specific bias with rater-specific tendencies; this reported setting change does not establish that simulations were rerun.

E4.justification: v5 newly reports that Dataset 1 trends survive median/mean rather than plurality aggregation and alternative aggregation across reference boundaries, without detailed sensitivity results. The scoring-pattern simulations, longer-scale robustness checks, violation-type analyses and qualitative examples already existed in v2.

E5.justification: v5 introduces Pearson-correlation estimates for relationships previously described qualitatively, including correlations above 0.7 with WRA and below 0.1 with MPA in the toxicity analysis. The 100-bootstrap-trial reporting, confidence-interval conventions and permutation-test significance reporting remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Crowd-reference values and demographic rankings change for both datasets, and toxicity gains IRT results. For example, White GenX men's MPA is 0.3903 in v2 Figure 3 and 0.4716 in v5 Figure 2 under different averaging protocols, preventing a same-setting performance interpretation. Guideline-reference, violation-type and simulation figures retain their results, as do the numerical appendix tables.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 replaces the latent-score model with rater/item biases and deterministic thresholds with rater-specific perception functions and non-decreasing probabilistic response functions. This substantively changes the formal model connecting severity, perception and ordinal scores. The two responsiveness inequalities and Appendix A proofs remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The contribution list removes high-impact-item prioritization as a headline contribution and introduces guidance for pluralistic safety alignment. The abstract and introduction foreground both existing datasets. The central claim that complementary responsiveness metrics capture granular and broader severity distinctions is retained.

C2.justification: Section 6 adds item audits and inclusion/weighting guidance for reward-model optimization, replacing v2's suggestion to reduce feedback collection from similarly responsive groups. The new Broader Impact statement explicitly discourages excluding groups for low responsiveness and recommends qualitative investigation. Section 3.1 also qualifies multidimensional applicability by requiring separate ratings per dimension.

D1.justification: v5 specifies the IRT model as the Graded Response Model and clarifies simulation percentile sampling as truncated normal. It omits v2's explicit item-replication instructions for constructing reference observations. The supplied metric code, CPU/complexity information and public-dataset availability remain essentially unchanged.

R1.justification: v5 adds Wang et al. (2025) and expands its positioning against IRT, arguing that shared latent calibration can obscure pluralistic variation. Most related work is retained. The additional Rastogi 2025 publication citation concerns the existing image dataset rather than a new dataset contribution.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten, reference construction receives its own subsection, and experiments are reorganized around two datasets. Toxicity moves into the main text, violation-type analyses move into the appendix, recommendations are rewritten, and a Broader Impact statement is added. The appendices are extensively reordered and consolidated.

P2.justification: Displays are extensively redistributed: v2 Figures 1 and 4 become appendix Figures 8 and 9, while toxicity Figure 12 becomes main-text Figure 3. Crowd-reference plots are redrawn with revised axes, group ordering and legends, including the added toxicity IRT curve. Tables, typography and page layout are reformatted for TMLR.

improvement.justification: v5 improves interpretability through more explicit probabilistic assumptions, an additional IRT comparison on toxicity, and actionable guidance against excluding demographic groups. Integrating the existing second case study also improves the narrative. These gains are limited by unresolved technical consistency: the newly stated MPA zero floor is absent from Appendix C code, and the revised simulation description retains the earlier plots without establishing a rerun.
